Correct
kor-rekt'
v. (to set right by discipline; to chastise in measure)
Latin corrigere, to make straight, from cor- and regere, to rule or direct. The English keeps the idea of straightening a thing that has bent, which is exactly the Hebrew use: correction is aimed at a crooked course, not at the destruction of the one corrected.

Biblical Definition

Jeremiah supplies the doctrine of this word in three sentences. First, the self-executing kind: “Thine own wickedness shall correct thee, and thy backslidings shall reprove thee” (Jer 2:19) — sin is its own schoolmaster, and God often needs no other rod than the natural harvest of the thing a man wanted. Second, the prayer of a man who knows he needs it: “O LORD, correct me, but with judgment; not in thine anger, lest thou bring me to nothing” (Jer 10:24). He does not ask to be spared correction; he asks for it in judgment rather than in wrath, which is precisely the distinction between fatherly chastisement and penal justice. Third, the promise: “I will correct thee in measure, and will not leave thee altogether unpunished” (Jer 30:11). In measure — weighed, limited, proportioned to the child and not to the offence in strict justice, because the strict justice fell at Calvary. The same word governs the home: “Correct thy son, and he shall give thee rest; yea, he shall give delight unto thy soul” (Pro 29:17), and Proverbs 23:13 forbids withholding it. And Psalm 94:10 settles the right of the Corrector: “He that chastiseth the heathen, shall not he correct?”

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines correct as to make right, to rectify what is wrong; and to chastise, to punish for the purpose of amendment.

expand to see more

CORRECT, v.t. To make right; to rectify; to bring to the standard of truth, justice or propriety.

1. To chastise; to punish for faults or deviations from moral rectitude; to discipline.

2. To obviate or remove whatever is wrong or inconvenient; to counteract, as an ill quality.

CORRECTION, n. Punishment; discipline; chastisement; that which corrects.

Key Scripture

Jer 10:24 — "O LORD, correct me, but with judgment; not in thine anger, lest thou bring me to nothing."

Jer 30:11 — "For I am with thee, saith the LORD, to save thee: though I make a full end of all nations whither I have scattered thee, yet will I not make a full end of thee: but I will correct thee in measure, and will not leave thee altogether unpunished."

Jer 2:19 — "Thine own wickedness shall correct thee, and thy backslidings shall reprove thee: know therefore and see that it is an evil thing and bitter, that thou hast forsaken the LORD thy God, and that my fear is not in thee, saith the Lord GOD of hosts."

Pro 29:17 — "Correct thy son, and he shall give thee rest; yea, he shall give delight unto thy soul."

Modern Corruption

Correction of children is now widely reclassified as harm; Proverbs makes withholding it the cruelty.

expand to see more

The dominant framework treats parental correction as a risk to be minimized, and reaches for the language of harm as the primary moral category. Scripture's categories are different and older: a child left uncorrected is not thereby protected but abandoned, because folly is bound in his heart and something must drive it out. Withhold not correction from the child (Pro 23:13) is a command to parents, and the promise attached to obeying it is rest and delight in the home. This is not license for anger. The very same Bible forbids provoking children to wrath, and the model of correction it gives is Jeremiah 30:11 — measured, purposeful, never to destruction, always aimed at restoring.

The deeper corruption is theological: a God who does not correct. Where fatherly chastisement is dropped from the doctrine of God, believers read every affliction either as divine anger or as meaningless accident, and both readings crush them. Hebrews 12 gives the third and true reading: whom the Lord loveth he chasteneth, and the son not chastened is the son not owned. Jeremiah's prayer is the right one — not spare me but correct me with judgment.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew yasar (H3256), to chastise, instruct, correct; musar (H4148), discipline, instruction; Greek paideuo (G3811), to train a child by discipline.

expand to see more

Hebrew yasar (H3256) — to discipline, chasten, instruct by correction; Jeremiah 10:24, 30:11, Proverbs 29:17.

Hebrew musar (H4148) — correction, discipline, instruction; the noun that runs through Proverbs 1-9.

Hebrew yakach (H3198) — to reprove, argue, set right; Jeremiah 2:19, thy backslidings shall reprove thee.

Greek paideuo (G3811) — to instruct a child, to chastise; Hebrews 12:6-10, 1 Corinthians 11:32.

Greek epanorthosis (G1882) — correction, setting straight again; 2 Timothy 3:16, profitable for correction.

Usage

"“Correct me, but with judgment; not in thine anger” — the believer's exact request."

"“I will correct thee in measure” — weighed, limited, fatherly."

"“Thine own wickedness shall correct thee” — sin as its own schoolmaster."
